questions.question: A light ray passes through the centre of curvature of a convex mirror. What happens to it after reflection?

options.text: It becomes parallel to the principal axis.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It retraces its own path.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Light rays passing through the center of curvature:** When a light ray passes through the **center of curvature** of a convex mirror, it is reflected back along the same path. This is due to the fact that the center of curvature lies on the normal to the mirror's surface, making the angle of incidence and reflection **equal to zero**.
 
• **Law of Reflection:** The phenomenon is explained by the **Law of Reflection**, which states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Since the ray strikes the mirror perpendicularly at the center of curvature, it retraces its path.
 
• **Convex mirror properties:** A convex mirror always diverges light rays. However, when a ray passes through the center of curvature, it behaves as if the mirror is locally flat at that point, leading to the retracing of the light ray.
 
• **Geometrical optics principle:** The center of curvature is a specific point on the principal axis equidistant from all points on the mirror's surface. This symmetry ensures that any ray passing through it reflects directly back.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is **It retraces its own path.**__*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Convex Mirror:**

 
 
• A convex mirror is a spherical mirror with the reflecting surface **bulging outward**.
 
• It is also known as a **diverging mirror** because it causes light rays to spread out after reflection.
 
• Convex mirrors are commonly used as **rearview mirrors** in vehicles due to their wide field of view.
 
 
 
• **Center of Curvature:**
 
 
• The center of curvature is the center of the sphere from which the mirror is a part.
 
• It lies outside the mirror for both convex and concave mirrors.
 
• For a convex mirror, the center of curvature is on the side opposite to the reflecting surface.
 
 
 
• **Focal Point and Principal Axis:**
 
 
• The **focal point** of a convex mirror is the point where reflected rays appear to diverge from. It is located on the principal axis between the mirror and the center of curvature.
 
• The **principal axis** is an imaginary line passing through the center of curvature and the pole of the mirror.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Convex Mirrors:**
 
 
• Used in **rearview mirrors** of vehicles to provide a wider field of view.
 
• Installed in **corridors, parking lots, and blind spots** for surveillance and safety purposes.
 
• Employed in **optical devices** like telescopes to correct image distortions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference between Convex and Concave Mirrors:**

 
 
• A convex mirror always forms a **virtual, erect, and diminished image** irrespective of the object's position.
 
• In contrast, a concave mirror can form **real or virtual images** depending on the object's position relative to the focal point and center of curvature.
 
 
 
• **Reflection from a Plane Surface:**
 
 
• When light reflects off a plane mirror, it follows the same fundamental **law of reflection** as for curved mirrors.
 
• However, in curved mirrors like convex mirrors, the curvature affects the direction of reflected rays.

• The **atomic mass of magnesium** is **24.305 u**, and the **atomic mass of oxygen** is **15.999 u**.
 
• The **molecular mass of magnesium oxide** is calculated as:

__
 
• **Magnesium (Mg):**

 
 
• Magnesium is a chemical element with the atomic number **12**.
 
• It is an **alkaline earth metal**, lightweight, and silvery-white in appearance.
 
• Magnesium is highly reactive in nature and is widely used in **alloys, batteries, and fertilizers**.
 
 
 
• **Oxygen (O):**
 
 
• Oxygen is a chemical element with the atomic number **8**.
 
• It is a highly reactive non-metal and is essential for the survival of most life forms on Earth.

• **Atomic Mass:** The atomic mass is the weighted average mass of the atoms in a naturally occurring element, measured in atomic mass units (u).
 
• **Molecular Mass:** The molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule.
 
• Magnesium oxide's composition is **1:1** for magnesium and oxygen atoms, making it a simple binary compound.
 
• It is a stable compound and does not decompose easily under normal conditions.

questions.question: What should be the position of the object, if a concave mirror forms a virtual, erect and enlarged image of the object?

options.text: The object is placed between the focus and the centre of curvature.
The object is placed at the centre of curvature of the mirror.
The object is placed at the focus of the mirror.
The object is placed between the pole and the focus of the mirror.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The object is placed between the pole and the focus of the mirror**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **concave mirror** can form different types of images depending on the position of the object.
 
• When the object is placed **between the pole (P)** and the **focus (F)** of the concave mirror, the image formed is **virtual, erect, and magnified**.
 
• This phenomenon occurs because the reflected rays appear to diverge and meet behind the mirror, creating a virtual image.
 
• The **enlarged virtual image** is seen on the same side of the mirror as the object.
 
• *Example:* This property of concave mirrors is used in applications like **makeup mirrors** and **dentist’s mirrors** to provide a magnified view.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Concave Mirror:**

 
 
• A concave mirror is a **spherical mirror** that has a reflecting surface on the inside of the sphere.
 
• It is also called a **converging mirror** as it focuses parallel rays of light to a single point known as the **focus**.
 
• Applications of concave mirrors include **telescopes, headlights, and shaving mirrors**.
 
 
 
• **Image Characteristics Based on Object Placement:**
 
 
• If the object is placed **at infinity**, the image is formed at the focus (F), and it is real, inverted, and highly diminished.
 
• When the object is placed **beyond the center of curvature (C)**, the image is formed between C and F, and it is real, inverted, and diminished.
 
• If the object is placed **at the center of curvature (C)**, the image is formed at C, and it is real, inverted, and of the same size as the object.
 
• When the object is placed **between C and F**, the image is formed beyond C, and it is real, inverted, and magnified.
 
• When the object is placed **at the focus (F)**, the image is formed at infinity, and it is real, inverted, and highly magnified.
 
• If the object is placed **between the pole (P) and focus (F)**, the image is virtual, erect, and magnified.
 
 
 
• **Key Terms:**
 
 
• **Focus (F):** The point where parallel rays of light converge after reflection from a concave mirror.
 
• **Center of Curvature (C):** The center of the sphere from which the mirror is a part.
 
• **Pole (P):** The geometric center of the mirror’s surface.
 
• **Principal Axis:** The straight line passing through the pole and the center of curvature.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Virtual and Magnified Images:**
 
 
• **Makeup Mirrors:** Concave mirrors are used to magnify facial features for better visibility while applying makeup.
 
• **Dentistry:** Dentists use concave mirrors to get an enlarged and clear view of a patient’s teeth.
 
• **Ophthalmology:** Used in diagnostic tools to examine the human eye.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Real Images:** Formed when light rays actually converge and meet after reflection; they are always inverted.
 
• **Virtual Images:** Formed when light rays appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror; they are always erect.
 
• **Magnification:** The degree to which the image size is larger or smaller than the object size, denoted by the formula **M = -v/u**, where **v** is the image distance and **u** is the object distance.
 
• **Mirror Formula:** The relationship between object distance (**u**), image distance (**v**), and focal length (**f**) is given by **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**.

questions.question: What is the atomic mass of oxygen?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**16 u**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Atomic Mass:** The atomic mass of an element is defined as the mass of its atom expressed in atomic mass units (**u**). For oxygen, the atomic mass is **16 u**.
 
• **Oxygen's Isotope:** The most abundant isotope of oxygen is **Oxygen-16**, which has 8 protons and 8 neutrons, resulting in an atomic mass of **16 u**.
 
• **Periodic Table:** Oxygen is represented by the symbol **O** in the periodic table and is located in Group 16 (Chalcogens) and Period 2.
 
• **Significance:** The atomic mass is crucial for chemical calculations, including determining the molar mass of compounds that include oxygen.
 
• **Incorrect Options:** **18 u** refers to the molecular mass of water (H₂O), **8 u** is incorrect as it only accounts for protons, and **12 u** corresponds to the atomic mass of carbon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Isotopes of Oxygen:** Oxygen exists in three isotopes: **Oxygen-16**, **Oxygen-17**, and **Oxygen-18**. Among these, **Oxygen-16** is the most abundant, comprising over **99.76%** of naturally occurring oxygen.
 
• **Properties:** Oxygen is a highly reactive non-metal and is essential for life. It is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust and atmosphere.
 
• **Applications:** Oxygen is widely used in industries such as **steel production**, **medical oxygen therapy**, and **water treatment**. It is also vital for combustion processes.
 
• **Molecular Oxygen:** Oxygen commonly exists as a diatomic molecule (**O₂**) in nature. The molecular mass of oxygen gas is **32 u** (16 u × 2).
 
• **Discovery:** Oxygen was discovered by **Carl Wilhelm Scheele** in 1772 and independently by **Joseph Priestley** in 1774. The name "oxygen" was coined by **Antoine Lavoisier**, who demonstrated its role in combustion and respiration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Atomic Mass Unit (u):** An atomic mass unit is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It is approximately **1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg**.
 
• **Periodic Table Context:** Oxygen is the eighth element in the periodic table, with an atomic number of **8**, representing its number of protons.
 
• **Role in Compounds:** Oxygen forms numerous compounds, including oxides, acids, and organic molecules. It is part of water (H₂O), which is essential for all forms of life.
 
• **Reactivity:** Oxygen readily forms bonds with other elements due to its high electronegativity (**3.44** on the Pauling scale).
 
• **Environmental Impact:** Oxygen is critical for maintaining life on Earth and is involved in processes such as **photosynthesis** and **respiration**. However, excessive oxygen in water bodies can lead to issues like **eutrophication**.

questions.question: A resistor of 4 Omega produces 64 J of heat every second. What is the potential difference across it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**16 V**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The problem involves calculating the **potential difference (V)** across a resistor using the given data of heat produced and resistance.
 
• The relationship between heat, current, and resistance is derived from the formula for power dissipation: **P = I²R**, where P is power, I is current, and R is resistance.
 
• Given that the resistor produces **64 J of heat every second**, this indicates that the **power (P)** is 64 W (since power is energy per unit time).
 
• To find the current (I), use the formula: **P = I²R**. Rearranging gives: **I = √(P/R)**. Substituting the values:

 I = √(64/4) = √16 = 4 A.
 
• Next, use Ohm’s Law: **V = IR**, to calculate the potential difference. Substituting the values:

 V = 4 × 4 = 16 V.
 
• **Hence, the correct answer is 16 V.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ohm’s Law:**

 
 
• Ohm's Law states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R).
 
• The mathematical expression is: **V = IR**.
 
• This law is fundamental in circuit analysis and is used to calculate voltage, current, or resistance in electrical circuits.
 
 
 
• **Power in Electrical Circuits:**
 
 
• Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an electric circuit. It is measured in **watts (W)**.
 
• The formula for power is: **P = V × I**, where P is power, V is voltage, and I is current.
 
• Alternatively, using Ohm's Law, power can also be expressed as: **P = I²R** or **P = V²/R**.
 
 
 
• **Resistance:**
 
 
• Resistance is a measure of the opposition to the flow of electric current in a circuit. It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**.
 
• Factors affecting resistance include the material, length, and cross-sectional area of the conductor, as well as temperature.
 
• Resistors are components specifically designed to provide a certain amount of resistance in electrical circuits.
 
 
 
• **Heat Produced by a Resistor:**
 
 
• When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat energy. This phenomenon is described by **Joule’s Law of Heating**.
 
• The heat produced is directly proportional to the square of the current, the resistance, and the time for which the current flows: **H = I²Rt**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Unit of Power:** The unit of power is **watt (W)**, where 1 watt equals 1 joule per second.
 
• **Unit of Resistance:** The unit of resistance is **ohm (Ω)**, named after the German physicist **Georg Simon Ohm**.
 
• **Practical Applications:** Understanding these concepts is essential for designing electrical appliances, power systems, and electronic devices.
 
• **Safety Note:** Excessive heat generated by resistors can damage circuits, so proper heat dissipation mechanisms, such as heat sinks or fans, are often employed.

questions.question: What is the longevity period of egg in the fallopian tube in case of failure of fertilisation in human females?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1-2 days**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In human females, after ovulation, the egg remains viable for fertilization for a period of **24 to 48 hours (1-2 days)**.
 
• The egg is released from the ovary and travels to the **fallopian tube**, where it waits for sperm for fertilization.
 
• If fertilization does not occur within this period, the egg degenerates and is absorbed by the body. ***Hence, the correct option is 1-2 days.***
 
• This limited viability is one of the key reasons why the timing of intercourse or artificial insemination is crucial for successful conception.
 
• The lifespan of the egg is significantly shorter compared to sperm, which can survive in the female reproductive tract for up to **5 days** under optimal conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ovulation Process:**

 
 
• Ovulation occurs mid-cycle, approximately on the **14th day** of a typical 28-day menstrual cycle.
 
• The process is triggered by a surge in **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** secreted by the pituitary gland.
 
• The released egg is encased within a structure called the **corona radiata** and is pushed into the fallopian tube by the fimbriae of the ovary.
 
 
 
• **Role of Fallopian Tubes:**
 
 
• The fallopian tubes are essential for transporting the egg from the ovary to the uterus.
 
• They are the site of fertilization, where the sperm meets the egg to form a **zygote**.
 
• Any blockage or damage to the fallopian tubes can lead to infertility.
 
 
 
• **Fertilization Window:**
 
 
• The fertile window typically spans **5-6 days**, including the day of ovulation and the days leading up to it.
 
• During this time, sexual intercourse or insemination has the highest probability of leading to pregnancy.
 
 
 
• **Hormonal Regulation:**
 
 
• The menstrual cycle is regulated by hormones such as **FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone)**, **LH (Luteinizing Hormone)**, **Estrogen**, and **Progesterone**.
 
• These hormones ensure the maturation of the egg, its release, and preparation of the uterine lining for implantation.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Sperm and Egg Lifespan:**
 
 
• While the egg’s lifespan is limited to **1-2 days**, sperm can survive for up to **5 days** in the female reproductive tract under favorable conditions.
 
• This difference in viability highlights the importance of timing in conception.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Menstrual Cycle Phases:**

 
 
• The menstrual cycle has four phases: **menstrual phase, follicular phase, ovulation phase, and luteal phase**.
 
• Ovulation is a critical phase for reproduction, occurring around the midpoint of the cycle.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Egg Viability:**
 
 
• Age plays a significant role, as **egg quality declines with age**, particularly after 35 years.
 
• Hormonal imbalances and lifestyle factors like stress, diet, and smoking can impact fertility.
 
 
 
• **Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART):**
 
 
• Techniques like **IVF (In Vitro Fertilization)** and **IUI (Intrauterine Insemination)** help couples with conception challenges.
 
• In IVF, eggs are fertilized outside the body and then implanted into the uterus.
 
 
 
• **Egg Freezing:**
 
 
• Egg freezing allows women to preserve their fertility for future use, especially if they plan to delay pregnancy.
 
• The frozen eggs can later be thawed, fertilized, and implanted as part of ART procedures.

questions.question: Which of the following tissues makes the plant hard and stiff?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sclerenchyma**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sclerenchyma** is a type of plant tissue that provides **mechanical support** to the plant and makes it **hard and stiff**. It is the main strengthening tissue in plants.
 
• The cells of sclerenchyma are characterized by their **thickened, lignified cell walls**, which provide rigidity and durability.
 
• Sclerenchyma cells are typically **dead at maturity**. They lack protoplasm, making them well-suited to their role as a support structure.
 
• There are two types of sclerenchyma cells: **fibers** (elongated cells) and **sclereids** (short, irregularly shaped cells). Both contribute to the hardness of plant parts, such as seed coats, nutshells, and vascular bundles.
 
• Common examples of sclerenchyma include **coconut husk fibers** and the gritty texture in guava or pear, which is due to sclereids.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Collenchyma:**

 
 
• Collenchyma cells have **unevenly thickened cell walls**, primarily composed of cellulose and pectin.
 
• This tissue provides **flexibility and mechanical support** to growing parts of the plant, such as stems and leaves.
 
• Unlike sclerenchyma, collenchyma cells are **living at maturity** and have a protoplasm.
 
 
 
• **Aerenchyma:**
 
 
• Aerenchyma is a specialized parenchyma tissue with large air spaces that facilitate **gas exchange** and buoyancy in aquatic plants.
 
• It is commonly found in plants like **water hyacinth** and **lotus**, where it helps the plant to float.
 
 
 
• **Chlorenchyma:**
 
 
• Chlorenchyma cells contain abundant **chloroplasts** and are involved in **photosynthesis**.
 
• This tissue is present in the mesophyll of leaves and other green parts of plants.
 
• Chlorenchyma contributes to the production of food in plants through the process of photosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **Sclerenchyma Characteristics:**
 
 
• **Location:** Found in stems, roots, vascular bundles, and hard parts like seed coats and nutshells.
 
• **Function:** Provides rigidity, durability, and mechanical strength to the plant.
 
• **Examples:** Coconut husk fibers, sclereids in pears, and the hard shell of nuts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Differences Between Sclerenchyma and Collenchyma:**

 
 
• Sclerenchyma cells are **dead** at maturity, while collenchyma cells are **living**.
 
• Sclerenchyma has **thick lignified walls**, whereas collenchyma walls are **unevenly thickened** and non-lignified.
 
• Collenchyma provides **flexibility**, while sclerenchyma provides **rigidity**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Sclerenchyma:**
 
 
• Used in **rope-making** due to the fibers' strength (e.g., jute and hemp).
 
• Provides structural support in **wood and bamboo** industries.

questions.question: A mother who is malnourished during pregnancy is likely to:

options.text: give birth to an underweight baby

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**give birth to an underweight baby**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A malnourished mother during pregnancy lacks essential nutrients such as **proteins, vitamins, and minerals**, which are crucial for the growth and development of the fetus.
 
• Malnutrition can lead to **intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)**, resulting in the birth of an underweight baby (weighing less than 2.5 kg).
 
• Underweight babies are at a higher risk of developing **health issues** such as weakened immunity, developmental delays, and chronic illnesses later in life.
 
• Prenatal malnutrition affects the **placental function**, reducing the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus, which directly impacts fetal weight and growth.
 
• Hence, ensuring a **balanced diet and proper prenatal care** is critical for the health of both the mother and the baby.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Nutrition in Pregnancy:**

 
 
• A balanced diet rich in **iron, calcium, folic acid, and proteins** is essential for fetal development.
 
• **Iron deficiency** in pregnant women can lead to anemia and low birth weight in babies.
 
• **Folic acid** prevents neural tube defects in the fetus.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Low Birth Weight:**
 
 
• Babies with low birth weight are more prone to **infections** due to a weaker immune system.
 
• They may face **difficulty in feeding, maintaining body temperature, and gaining weight.**
 
 
 
• **Global Statistics on Maternal Malnutrition:**
 
 
• According to the **World Health Organization (WHO)**, approximately **20 million babies** are born with low birth weight annually, primarily in developing countries.
 
• Maternal malnutrition is a significant contributor to this issue, especially in low-income regions.
 
 
 
• **Preventive Measures:**
 
 
• **Antenatal care programs** can help monitor maternal health and provide nutritional supplements.
 
• Fortification of staple foods and public health campaigns can address dietary deficiencies in pregnant women.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison of Options:**

 
 
• **Option 1 - Have a stronger immune system:** Malnutrition weakens the immune system instead of strengthening it. This is incorrect.
 
• **Option 2 - Have a faster delivery:** Malnutrition does not directly cause faster delivery. Preterm birth may occur in malnourished mothers, but it is not equivalent to faster delivery. This is incorrect.
 
• **Option 3 - Give birth to an underweight baby:** This is the most accurate option as maternal malnutrition is directly linked to low birth weight. This is correct.
 
• **Option 4 - Produce more milk:** Malnutrition reduces the mother's capacity to produce sufficient milk for the newborn. This is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives in India:**
 
 
• The **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** scheme provides supplementary nutrition to pregnant and lactating mothers.

questions.question: Which of the following facilitates the communication between the central nervous system and the other parts of the body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Peripheral nervous system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)** serves as the communication network between the **Central Nervous System (CNS)**, comprising the brain and spinal cord, and the rest of the body.
 
• It is responsible for transmitting **sensory inputs** from various parts of the body to the CNS and relaying **motor commands** from the CNS to the muscles and glands for action.
 
• The PNS is divided into two primary components: **Somatic Nervous System** (controls voluntary movements) and **Autonomic Nervous System** (regulates involuntary functions like heart rate and digestion).
 
• **Cranial nerves** and **spinal nerves**, which are part of the PNS, connect the CNS to the limbs, organs, and external environment.
 
• It plays a crucial role in enabling **reflex actions, sensory perception, and motor coordination**, ensuring smooth functioning of the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Central Nervous System (CNS):**

 
 
• The CNS includes the **brain** and **spinal cord**, which are responsible for processing sensory information, making decisions, and controlling body movements.
 
• The brain is the command center, while the spinal cord acts as the conduit for transmitting signals to and from the PNS.
 
• It is protected by the **skull** and **vertebral column**, as well as layers of meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.
 
 
 
• **Somatic Nervous System:**
 
 
• Part of the PNS that controls **voluntary movements** of skeletal muscles.
 
• It enables conscious activities such as walking, running, and grabbing objects.
 
• It includes afferent nerves (sensory) and efferent nerves (motor) to regulate interaction with the external environment.
 
 
 
• **Autonomic Nervous System:**
 
 
• Another division of the PNS that regulates **involuntary functions** like heart rate, breathing, and digestion.
 
• Divided into **sympathetic** (activates "fight or flight" response) and **parasympathetic** (promotes "rest and digest" functions).
 
• Helps maintain **homeostasis** by managing internal processes automatically.
 
 
 
• **Spinal Cord:**
 
 
• The spinal cord is part of the CNS but works closely with the PNS to transmit signals.
 
• It is protected by the **vertebral column** and serves as the main communication pathway between the brain and the peripheral nerves.
 
• It controls reflex actions independently of the brain through reflex arcs.
 
 
 
• **Voluntary and Involuntary Muscles:**
 
 
• **Voluntary muscles** are controlled by the somatic nervous system and are involved in conscious movements.
 
• **Involuntary muscles**, such as smooth muscles and cardiac muscles, are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.
 
• Though important for body functions, they do not directly facilitate communication between the CNS and other body parts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Functions of PNS:**

 
 
• Connects the CNS to limbs and organs.
 
• Facilitates sensory input and motor output.
 
• Ensures coordination between voluntary and involuntary bodily functions.
 
 
 
• **Cranial Nerves:**
 
 
• There are **12 cranial nerves** in the PNS that control sensory and motor functions in the head and neck.
 
• Examples include the optic nerve (vision) and vagus nerve (parasympathetic control).
 
 
 
• **Spinal Nerves:**
 
 
• **31 pairs** of spinal nerves originate from the spinal cord and regulate sensory and motor functions throughout the body.
 
• These nerves are categorized into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions.
 
 
 
• **Diseases Affecting the PNS:**
 
 
• Peripheral neuropathy, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and nerve compression syndromes can disrupt PNS functions.
 
• Effective treatment relies on early diagnosis and proper intervention.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the mitochondria in a plant cell?

options.text: Mitochondria does not have its own DNA.
The mitochondrial inner membrane is deeply folded.
Mitochondria has a single membranous covering.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The mitochondrial inner membrane is deeply folded**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mitochondria** are double-membraned organelles found in both plant and animal cells. They are known as the "powerhouses of the cell" because they generate energy in the form of **ATP (adenosine triphosphate)**.
 
• The inner membrane of mitochondria is deeply folded into structures called **cristae**. These folds increase the surface area for biochemical processes such as **oxidative phosphorylation**, which is crucial for energy production. Hence, this statement is **correct**.
 
• Mitochondria have their own **DNA**, which allows them to replicate and produce some of their own proteins independently of the cell nucleus. The statement "Mitochondria does not have its own DNA" is therefore **incorrect**.
 
• Mitochondria do not perform photosynthesis. Photosynthesis occurs in **chloroplasts**, which are organelles specific to plant cells. Thus, the statement "Mitochondria performs photosynthesis" is **incorrect**.
 
• Mitochondria have a **double membranous covering**, not a single membrane. The outer membrane is smooth, while the inner membrane is folded into cristae. Hence, the statement "Mitochondria has a single membranous covering" is **incorrect**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Mitochondria:**

 
 
• Mitochondria have two membranes: an **outer membrane** and an **inner membrane**.
 
• The inner membrane has folds called **cristae**, which are essential for increasing the surface area for metabolic activities.
 
• The space between the inner and outer membranes is called the **intermembrane space**, while the space inside the inner membrane is the **matrix**.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Mitochondria:**
 
 
• **Energy production:** Mitochondria generate ATP through the process of cellular respiration, primarily in the **electron transport chain** located in the cristae.
 
• **Apoptosis:** Mitochondria play a role in programmed cell death by releasing molecules like **cytochrome c**.
 
• **Calcium storage:** Mitochondria help regulate calcium levels in cells.
 
• **Metabolism:** They are involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
 
 
 
• **Unique Features of Mitochondria:**
 
 
• Mitochondria have their own **DNA** and **ribosomes**, enabling them to synthesize some of their own proteins.
 
• They are thought to have originated from an ancient symbiotic relationship with bacteria, as per the **endosymbiotic theory**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Chloroplasts:**
 
 
• Both mitochondria and chloroplasts have **double membranes** and their own **DNA**.
 
• While mitochondria are involved in **energy production** through cellular respiration, chloroplasts perform **photosynthesis** to convert light energy into chemical energy.
 
• Chloroplasts are exclusive to plants and algae, whereas mitochondria are found in almost all eukaryotic cells.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Electron Transport Chain:** The **ETC** is located in the inner membrane of mitochondria and plays a key role in **oxidative phosphorylation**, producing ATP.
 
• **Matrix:** The mitochondrial matrix contains **enzymes** that are crucial for the **Krebs cycle**, which is another step in energy production.
 
• **Endosymbiotic Theory:** The theory suggests that mitochondria evolved from free-living bacteria that entered into a symbiotic relationship with ancestral eukaryotic cells.
 
• **Diseases:** Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can lead to various disorders, such as **mitochondrial myopathy** and **Leigh syndrome**.
 
• **Adaptations:** The number of mitochondria in a cell varies depending on its energy requirements. For instance, muscle cells have a higher concentration of mitochondria.

questions.question: Which of the following non-metals exhibits a metallic lustre despite being chemically non-metallic?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iodine**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Iodine** is a non-metal but exhibits a **metallic lustre**. This is a unique characteristic among non-metals.
 
• The metallic lustre of iodine is due to the **reflection of light** by its closely packed molecules arranged in a crystalline structure.
 
• Iodine appears as a **shiny, dark gray or purple solid**, which is why it is often mistaken for a metal based on its appearance.
 
• Unlike metals, iodine is brittle and does not exhibit properties like ductility or malleability, affirming its classification as a non-metal.
 
• Iodine sublimates upon heating, transitioning directly from a solid to a purple vapor, which is a characteristic property of non-metals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Sulphur:**

 
 
• It is a **brittle yellow solid** at room temperature.
 
• It does not exhibit metallic lustre and is classified as a **non-metal**.
 
• Commonly used in the production of **sulfuric acid, fertilizers, and fireworks**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Phosphorus:**
 
 
• Exists in several allotropic forms, such as **white, red, and black phosphorus**.
 
• It does not exhibit metallic lustre; instead, white phosphorus is waxy and translucent, while red phosphorus is powdery.
 
• It is essential for biological processes and is a key component of **DNA, RNA, and ATP**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Nitrogen:**
 
 
• Nitrogen is a **colorless, odorless gas** at room temperature.
 
• It does not exhibit metallic lustre and is found abundantly in the **Earth’s atmosphere (78%)**.
 
• It plays a crucial role in the synthesis of **proteins and nucleic acids** in living organisms.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Iodine:**
 
 
• Iodine is a **halogen** and belongs to Group 17 of the periodic table.
 
• It is widely used in **medicine** as an antiseptic and in the **iodization of salt** to prevent iodine deficiency.
 
• It has a **relatively high atomic number (53)** among non-metals, which contributes to its metallic appearance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Why Iodine Exhibits Metallic Lustre:**

 
 
• The metallic appearance of iodine is due to the interaction of light with its **delocalized electrons** in the crystalline structure.
 
• This phenomenon is rare among non-metals, making iodine a unique element in terms of its physical properties.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Iodine:**
 
 
• Used in **diagnostic imaging** (iodine-based contrast agents).
 
• Essential in the production of **thyroid hormones**, which regulate metabolism.
 
• Serves as a catalyst in various **chemical reactions**.

questions.question: Why is it impossible for two magnetic field lines to cross each other at a single point?

options.text: Because they repel each other due to like polarity
Because it would imply the compass needle could point in two directions simultaneously
Because they are always parallel inside the magnet
Because the magnetic field strength would be zero at that point

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because it would imply the compass needle could point in two directions simultaneously**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Magnetic field lines** represent the direction and strength of a magnetic field at a given point. They are conceptual tools used to visualize magnetic forces.
 
• **Two magnetic field lines never cross each other** because if they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection, there are two different directions of the magnetic field. This is physically impossible as the magnetic field at any point can have only one direction.
 
• If two field lines intersected, a **compass needle placed at that point** would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is not feasible. *Hence, the correct answer is that it would imply the compass needle could point in two directions simultaneously.*
 
• Field lines are **continuous curves**, starting from the north pole of a magnet and ending at its south pole, without any abrupt changes or intersections.
 
• Magnetic field lines are **non-intersecting by nature**, ensuring a unique and consistent representation of the field’s direction and magnitude.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Magnetic Field Lines Characteristics:**

 
 
• **Closed Loops:** Magnetic field lines form closed loops. They emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet, while inside the magnet, they go from the south pole to the north pole.
 
• **Density Representation:** The density of magnetic field lines indicates the strength of the field. The closer the lines, the stronger the magnetic field in that region.
 
• **Non-Intersection:** As explained above, magnetic field lines do not intersect because a unique direction of the magnetic field is required at every point.
 
 
 
• **Compass Needle and Magnetic Fields:**
 
 
• A compass needle aligns itself along the direction of the magnetic field at any given point, helping visualize the field lines.
 
• If field lines intersected, the compass needle would experience conflicting forces, leading to ambiguous alignment, which does not occur in reality.
 
 
 
• **Other Incorrect Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Option 1:** Magnetic field lines do not repel each other due to like polarity. This is incorrect because field lines represent the direction of the field, not physical entities that repel.
 
• **Option 3:** Magnetic field lines are not always parallel inside the magnet. Instead, they form continuous loops, transitioning from south to north inside the magnet.
 
• **Option 4:** Magnetic field strength is not zero at the point where two lines could cross; the issue is with direction, not magnitude.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Magnetic Field Lines:**
 
 
• They are used to visualize the behavior of magnetic fields in devices like motors, transformers, and magnetic storage systems.
 
• Field lines help in understanding the magnetic effects in Earth’s magnetic field, solenoids, and electromagnets.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Magnetic Field Line Experiments:** Use of iron filings or compass needles to trace field lines around a magnet demonstrates their non-intersecting nature.
 
• **Earth’s Magnetic Field:** Earth’s magnetic field lines also follow the same rules, forming a dipole structure with non-intersecting lines.
 
• **Technological Implications:** Magnetic field visualization is crucial in designing and analyzing magnetic circuits, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and other applications.
 
• **Historical Note:** The concept of magnetic field lines was introduced by **Michael Faraday**, who laid the foundation for understanding electromagnetic phenomena.

questions.question: A yellow luminous flame is usually an indication of which of the following?

options.text: Incomplete combustion with unburnt carbon particles

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Incomplete combustion with unburnt carbon particles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **yellow luminous flame** is a clear indicator of **incomplete combustion**. This occurs when there is insufficient oxygen available for the fuel to combust completely.
 
• During incomplete combustion, **unburnt carbon particles** are released into the flame. These particles become heated and emit a yellow glow, giving the flame its characteristic color.
 
• Complete combustion, in contrast, results in a **blue flame** due to the efficient burning of the fuel, producing only carbon dioxide and water as byproducts. Hence, the yellow flame is not a sign of complete combustion.
 
• The formation of carbon dioxide is primarily associated with complete combustion, where hydrocarbons react fully with oxygen, and it does not contribute to the yellow color of the flame.
 
• The combustion of metals generally produces a bright white or colored flame depending on the metal but does not result in a yellow luminous flame. Therefore, this option is irrelevant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Incomplete Combustion:**

 
 
• Occurs when there is a lack of oxygen supply during the burning of fuel.
 
• Produces byproducts such as **carbon monoxide (CO)**, unburnt carbon particles (soot), and sometimes other hydrocarbons.
 
• It is less efficient and can be hazardous due to the release of carbon monoxide, a toxic gas.
 
• Examples include burning coal or wood in a poorly ventilated space.
 
 
 
• **Complete Combustion:**
 
 
• Requires adequate oxygen for the fuel to burn completely.
 
• Produces water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) as byproducts.
 
• The flame is typically blue due to the absence of unburnt carbon particles.
 
• Examples include the burning of natural gas in a gas stove or a well-tuned engine.
 
 
 
• **Combustion of Metals:**
 
 
• Metals like magnesium produce a bright white flame when combusted.
 
• Certain metals give distinct flame colors, e.g., sodium produces a yellow flame, copper produces green, etc.
 
• These flames are not related to incomplete combustion but rather the excitation of metal atoms.
 
 
 
• **Flame Characteristics:**
 
 
• The color of a flame can indicate the type of combustion:
 
 
• **Blue Flame:** Complete combustion, high temperature, efficient burning.
 
• **Yellow Flame:** Incomplete combustion, presence of soot, lower temperature.
 
 
 
• A yellow flame is often observed in candles or kerosene lamps.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hazards of Incomplete Combustion:**

 
 
• Releases **carbon monoxide (CO)**, which is a colorless, odorless, and highly toxic gas.
 
• Contributes to **air pollution** due to the release of particulate matter and other harmful gases.
 
• Leads to energy wastage as the fuel does not burn completely, reducing efficiency.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Flame Analysis:**
 
 
• Used in **chemical analysis** to identify elements based on the flame color they produce.
 
• Applied in industries to monitor combustion efficiency in furnaces and burners.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true according to the First Law of Motion?

options.text: A person continues to move forward when a car stops suddenly.
A car accelerates when the engine is started.
A stone falling freely under gravity.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A person continues to move forward when a car stops suddenly.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The First Law of Motion**, also known as Newton's First Law or the Law of Inertia, states that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force.
 
• When a car stops suddenly, a person inside the car continues to move forward due to **inertia**. This is because the body tends to maintain its state of motion unless an external force (like a seatbelt) acts on it. Hence, this statement is correct.
 
• A rocket launching upward does not directly illustrate the First Law of Motion but is instead an example of **Newton's Third Law**, which involves action and reaction forces. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• A car accelerating when the engine is started demonstrates the application of a net external force, which aligns with Newton's Second Law of Motion (Force = mass × acceleration). Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• A stone falling freely under gravity illustrates Newton's Second Law since the acceleration due to gravity acts on the stone. It is not an example of the First Law. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia):**

 
 
• An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.
 
• This law emphasizes the concept of **inertia**, which is the resistance of an object to changes in its state of motion.
 
 
 
• **Inertia:**
 
 
• Inertia is the property of a body due to which it resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.
 
• Example: When a train suddenly stops, passengers inside experience a forward motion because their bodies resist the sudden change in motion.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Second Law of Motion:**
 
 
• This law states that the force acting on an object is equal to the mass of the object times its acceleration (F = ma).
 
• Example: A car accelerating demonstrates the application of a net force.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Third Law of Motion:**
 
 
• This law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
 
• Example: The upward motion of a rocket is due to the downward expulsion of gases, which creates an equal and opposite reaction force.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Newton's First Law:**
 
 
• Seatbelts in cars are designed to counter inertia, preventing passengers from continuing forward motion during sudden stops.
 
• Tablecloth trick: Quickly pulling a tablecloth from under dishes without moving them illustrates inertia.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Significance of Inertia:**

 
 
• It explains why passengers in a moving vehicle lurch forward when the vehicle comes to a sudden stop.
 
• It is crucial in understanding the dynamics of motion in various systems, from vehicles to celestial bodies.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Newton's First Law was influenced by the earlier work of **Galileo Galilei**, who studied motion and the principle of inertia.
 
• Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion in his seminal work **"Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica"**, published in **1687**.

questions.question: Select the correct property of micelles in soap that help them to interact with water:

options.text: both hydrophilic head and hydrophobhic tail

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**hydrophilic head**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Micelles** are tiny spherical structures formed by soap molecules in water. They are formed when the soap concentration in water crosses a critical micelle concentration.
 
• Each soap molecule has two distinct parts: a **hydrophobic tail** (water-repelling) and a **hydrophilic head** (water-attracting).
 
• The **hydrophilic head**__ of the soap molecule interacts with water molecules because it is polar in nature, allowing micelles to remain suspended in water.
 
• When soap is added to water, its **hydrophobic tail avoids water** and clusters together, while the **hydrophilic head faces outward, interacting with water**. This arrangement creates a stable micelle structure.
 
• The ability of micelles to interact with water and trap oily dirt is attributed to the polar nature of the __**hydrophilic head**__, which forms a strong interaction with water molecules.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Soap Molecules:**

 
 
• Soap molecules are composed of a long hydrocarbon chain (hydrophobic tail) and a carboxylate ion (hydrophilic head).
 
• The hydrophobic tail is nonpolar and repels water, while the hydrophilic head is polar and interacts with water molecules.
 
 
 
• **Formation of Micelles:**
 
 
• When soap is added to water, the molecules arrange themselves in a spherical structure called a micelle.
 
• In a micelle, the hydrophilic heads face outward toward the water, and the hydrophobic tails cluster inward, avoiding water.
 
 
 
• **Cleaning Action of Soap:**
 
 
• The hydrophobic tail attaches to oily dirt, while the hydrophilic head remains in contact with water.
 
• This action forms an emulsion, breaking down the grease into smaller droplets that can be washed away with water.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Hydrophilic Head:**
 
 
• The hydrophilic head ensures that soap molecules remain dispersed in water, preventing the micelles from aggregating and settling at the bottom.
 
• It also helps in the removal of dirt by solubilizing it into water.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Micelles:**
 
 
• Micelles are widely used in cleaning, emulsification, and even in drug delivery systems in pharmaceuticals.
 
• Their unique structure allows them to trap hydrophobic substances like oils and grease and interact with water simultaneously.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hydrophobic Tail:**

 
 
• The hydrophobic tail is made of a long hydrocarbon chain, which repels water.
 
• It plays a critical role in trapping grease and oil but does not interact directly with water.
 
 
 
• **Hydrophilic Head:**
 
 
• The hydrophilic head is ionic or polar in nature, allowing it to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
 
• This property is crucial for the formation of micelles and their interaction with water.
 
 
 
• **Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC):**
 
 
• Micelles form only when the concentration of soap in water exceeds a certain threshold known as the Critical Micelle Concentration.
 
• Below this concentration, soap molecules remain dispersed and do not form micelles.

questions.question: What do we call the motion of an object that travels equal distances in equal intervals of time, even when the time intervals are very small?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uniform motion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Uniform motion** refers to the motion of an object that covers **equal distances in equal intervals of time**, regardless of how small the time intervals are.
 
• In uniform motion, the **velocity of the object remains constant**. This means that there is no change in speed or direction over time.
 
• Examples of uniform motion include a car moving at a constant speed on a straight road or light traveling through a vacuum.
 
• This type of motion is characterized by a **straight-line graph of displacement vs. time**, indicating a constant rate of change in position.
 
• Uniform motion is an **idealized concept** often used in physics to simplify real-world scenarios, as most motions in real life are non-uniform due to external forces like friction and air resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Accelerated motion:**

 
 
• In accelerated motion, an object’s **velocity changes over time** due to the application of a net force.
 
• Acceleration can be **positive (speeding up)** or **negative (slowing down)**.
 
• Examples include a car speeding up when the accelerator is pressed or a ball falling under the influence of gravity.
 
 
 
• **Circular motion:**
 
 
• Circular motion refers to the movement of an object along a **circular path**.
 
• It can be uniform (constant speed) or non-uniform (changing speed).
 
• In uniform circular motion, although the speed is constant, the **direction of velocity changes continuously**, resulting in centripetal acceleration directed towards the center of the circle.
 
• Examples include the motion of planets around the sun or a car taking a circular turn.
 
 
 
• **Non-uniform motion:**
 
 
• In non-uniform motion, an object covers **unequal distances in equal intervals of time**, or its speed/direction changes over time.
 
• This is the most common type of motion observed in real-life scenarios due to external factors like friction and varying forces.
 
• An example is a vehicle moving in heavy traffic where it speeds up, slows down, or stops intermittently.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Uniform Motion:**
 
 
• Uniform motion is used in navigation systems to calculate distance and time accurately.
 
• It is also an important concept in designing transportation systems and in the study of celestial mechanics.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Graphs of Motion:**

 
 
• In uniform motion, a graph of **distance vs. time** is a straight line with a constant slope.
 
• For non-uniform motion, the graph may curve or have varying slopes, indicating changes in speed or direction.
 
 
 
• **Equation for Uniform Motion:**
 
 
• The equation of motion is given by **s = vt**, where **s** is displacement, **v** is velocity, and **t** is time.
 
 
 
• **Difference from Real-World Motion:**
 
 
• Uniform motion is an **idealized concept**, while real-world motions are often influenced by external forces like friction and air resistance, making them non-uniform.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about modern fish farming?

options.text: All fish seeds are collected from rivers
Hormones are used for fish breeding
Enzymes are used to help fish grow bigger
Fish farming cannot be done in ponds

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hormones are used for fish breeding**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hormones are used for fish breeding:**

 
 
• In modern aquaculture, artificial breeding methods often utilize **hormones** to induce spawning in fish species that do not breed naturally in captivity.
 
• The hormonal injections, such as **Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (HCG)** or pituitary extracts, stimulate the reproductive organs to mature and release eggs or sperm for fertilization.
 
• This technique is crucial for breeding commercially important species like **carps, catfish, and tilapia**. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
 
 
• **All fish seeds are collected from rivers:**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as modern fish farming relies on hatcheries for seed production rather than river collection. Collecting seeds from rivers is traditional and unsustainable for large-scale production.
 
• Hatcheries ensure a controlled and consistent supply of **fish seeds** with better survival rates.
 
 
 
• **Enzymes are used to help fish grow bigger:**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect. Enzymes are not directly used to enhance fish growth. Instead, fish growth depends on balanced nutrition, genetics, and environmental conditions.
 
• While enzymes may be added to fish feed to improve digestion, they do not directly contribute to increasing the size of fish.
 
 
 
• **Fish farming cannot be done in ponds:**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect. Fish farming is extensively practiced in **ponds, tanks, and cages** across the globe.
 
• Pond aquaculture is a popular and efficient method for rearing various fish species such as **carps, catfish, and tilapia**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Hormones in Aquaculture:**

 
 
• Hormonal induction is a widely used method to overcome problems like seasonal breeding and poor reproductive performance in captivity.
 
• Examples of hormones used include **Ovaprim**, a synthetic hormone widely used for breeding Indian major carps and other species.
 
• This method ensures a continuous supply of fish seeds for commercial aquaculture.
 
 
 
• **Hatchery Systems in Fish Farming:**
 
 
• Hatcheries are controlled environments designed to breed, hatch, and raise fish larvae until they are ready for stocking in grow-out systems.
 
• They provide a reliable source of fingerlings and help reduce the dependence on wild fish populations.
 
• Countries like **India, China, and Vietnam** have large-scale hatcheries for fish seed production.
 
 
 
• **Fish Nutrition and Growth:**
 
 
• Fish growth is influenced by a combination of genetic, nutritional, and environmental factors.
 
• Modern aquaculture uses formulated feeds with balanced levels of protein, lipids, vitamins, and minerals to optimize fish growth.
 
• Enzymes in feed, such as proteases and phytases, improve nutrient absorption but do not directly increase fish size.
 
 
 
• **Types of Aquaculture Systems:**
 
 
• Pond aquaculture: Most common and cost-effective system for rearing freshwater fish.
 
• Tank or recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS): Advanced systems used to maintain water quality and control environmental factors.
 
• Cage aquaculture: Practiced in open water bodies like lakes and reservoirs for species like **salmon** and **trout**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Aquaculture Production:**

 
 
• According to the **FAO's 2022 report**, aquaculture contributes over **50%** of the world’s fish supply.
 
• Major contributors include countries like **China (60%), India, Indonesia, and Vietnam**.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Sustainability in Aquaculture:**
 
 
• Practices like **integrated multi-trophic aquaculture** (IMTA) and biofloc technology are gaining traction to minimize environmental impacts.
 
• Efforts are being made to reduce dependence on wild fish for feed by using plant-based alternatives and microbial proteins.
